idiom_name: Boost.Interprocess managed_shared_memory with find_or_construct/find by name
implementation_notes: The pattern is assembled from library pieces rather than provided as a component: Boost.Interprocess gives the store - managed_shared_memory, with find_or_construct/find/destroy keyed by a c-string and a segment size fixed at construction - while the seam code (take the payload out of the message, put the key in, redeem it later) stays yours. Inside one process the store hop is unnecessary, because std::shared_ptr (or a move) already passes a reference and copying it is what the pattern exists to avoid. Keep the key cheap (std::string_view, a small id struct): a claim check that allocates or copies on every message reintroduces the cost the pattern removed, and the classic shared-memory form is only justified when the payload must cross a process boundary.
pitfalls: The segment size is fixed when it is created: find_or_construct fails or throws once the segment is full, and named objects cannot grow in place, so size for the worst case or shard by key.

Pointers inside a managed segment must be offset_ptr (or segment-allocated containers): storing raw pointers or std::string members in shared objects corrupts data as soon as the segment is mapped at a different address in another process.
Destructors of named objects are not run when the segment is destroyed, so anything that holds a lock or a resource inside the segment leaks unless destroy<T> is called explicitly.
Concurrent producers must serialise find_or_construct (segment mutex family or an external lock), or two processes can build the same named object and lose one payload.
